Pele Yoetz 217:10: In any case, one who is compelled to be without his wife, or who is on a journey, or during her time of niddah, should be firm in strengthening himself to build a fence for himself and make a covenant with his eyes, and not to converse excessively with women — for even regarding his own wife they said, how much more so [with other women], etc. — and let him do whatever is in his power to do; perhaps there is hope to be saved from the transgression and from improper thoughts of sin, and one who comes to purify himself is helped [from Heaven] (Shabbat 104a).
Pele Yoetz 217:11: Included in this is to purify oneself from speech that leads to improper musings, as it is written (Deuteronomy 23:10), “And you shall guard yourself from every evil thing.” For besides the severity of the prohibition against vulgar speech, as written in its place, there is more: it brings a person to improper musing; therefore, even speaking words of Torah on matters between a man and his wife, the modest hold back their hand, especially in front of many unlearned people. And every prudent person should act with knowledge and weigh in the balance a time to be silent and a time to speak.
Pele Yoetz 217:12: And a woman must be especially and extra careful not to cause others to stumble, for that woman will bear her own sin and takes the leading share of blame, for one who causes another to sin is worse and more bitter than one who kills him; therefore she must be careful not to go out adorned in front of men, and let all her glory be within, like a king's daughter. And I praise the sons of Ishmael in this matter, that they conceal their wives from every man. And all the more so, she should not nurse her son with her breasts exposed in front of many people. Likewise she should be careful not to lift the hem of her garments and not to put her hand under her apron to scratch herself in front of men. Likewise she should not recite the blessing “Asher Yatzar” aloud in front of men, and needless to say she should not enter the privy in front of men. All this and more — every woman of a wise heart and God-fearing who is extra careful in this shall be praised. And above all, how good it is that she precede with prayer at a time of trouble and pour out her soul before the Lord every day that He guide her with good counsel, so that no guilt come about through her, as recounted in the Talmud, for we learn the fear of sin from a maiden (Sotah 22a). (And on this too I have lifted my hand and included it in my prayer book, with Heaven's help.)
Pele Yoetz 217:13: And our sages, of blessed memory, warned of several matters in order to prevent one from coming to improper musing, such as not gazing at an animal, beast, or fowl while mating, and not sitting on a bed known to be one where a man and his wife lie, and not gazing at a woman's little finger. And they said (Berachot 24a) that whoever gazes at a woman's little finger is as though gazing at her private place. And they forbade making any use of a woman at all, or asking after her welfare, or conversing excessively with her, and certainly forbade her pouring a cup for him, making his bed, or washing his face, hands, or feet, which is forbidden to accept from any woman except one's own wife when she is ritually pure, as explained by the halachic authorities (Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer, sec. 21). And there are several such matters that our sages, of blessed memory, forbade in order to prevent improper musing, yet the masses are not careful about them. And even if a person says of himself that he does these things with an empty heart and escapes the actual musing, in any case he does not escape the transgression, for he transgresses the words of the Sages and arouses the evil inclination within him. And they said (Niddah 13b) that one who deliberately induces his own emission should be under a ban, because he arouses the evil inclination within him. Therefore let a man be firm in strengthening himself to fulfill the words of the Sages and add fence upon fence and safeguard upon safeguard for himself according to what kind of person he is, and whoever is most diligent in standing guard is to be praised. As we find with our holy sages, who used to tell their students, “Move aside for my daughter, for my daughter-in-law,” as brought in the Talmud (Kiddushin 81b). And the Lord will not withhold good from those who walk in innocence.
Pele Yoetz 218:1: Massa U'Matan (Business Dealings) — It is known that the first question asked at the Day of Judgment is, “Did you conduct business with integrity?” (Shabbat 31a; Sanhedrin 5a). And now, through our many sins, men of integrity have perished, saying vain arguments — that in this age a person's sustenance is difficult, and whoever wishes to conduct himself with faith and integrity cannot even eat bread with salt — and thereby it has become as though permitted to commit injustice, speak falsehood, defraud, steal, rob, encroach on boundaries, and many other evils, besides neglect of Torah and communal prayer, desecration of Shabbat, and the like, with no one taking to heart to regret the evil. Woe to people from the Day of Judgment. And it was not for nothing that they said (Menachot 29b), “Why was the World to Come created with the letter yud [the smallest letter]? Because the righteous within it are few,” for the entire Torah is included in faith, as it is written (Habakkuk 2:4), “And the righteous shall live by his faith.” And a person is recognized by his pocket, for one who believes in the Lord — that He gives strength to do valiantly, and that all of a person's sustenance is fixed for him from Rosh Hashanah (Beitzah 15a) by the mouth of the Most High — will not believe that by transgressing the mouth of the Lord he will succeed in his ways, God forbid to even mention it; and if he does succeed, it is certainly, without any doubt, wealth kept by its owner to his own harm, besides his punishment which is kept for him for the World to Come. And if you see an upright man who walks in the way of the good and conducts his business with integrity, whose sustenance is meager, Heaven forbid to believe that there is a righteous man perishing in his righteousness, God forbid — shall the Judge of all the earth not do justice? Heaven forbid; rather, His dealings are measured [with purpose]. And whoever believes truly in the Lord with a whole heart will believe with complete faith that the Rock, His work is perfect, all His ways are justice, and whatever the Merciful One does, He does for the good, so that it will ultimately be well for him, his understanding being good. And it is true that all of Israel are believers, children of believers, but faith alone is not the essential thing — all depends on the abundance of deeds that demonstrate the faith, as I have also written above under the entry Emunah.
Pele Yoetz 219:1: Minhag (Custom) — The saying of our sages, of blessed memory, is known (Shemot Rabbah 47:5): “When you go to a city, follow its custom” — one should not deviate from local custom. And great is the power of custom, to the point that they said (Massechet Soferim 14:18), “Custom overrides halachah.” And it is true that there are bad customs that ought to be abolished, but a scale and balance of judgment are needed: if there is a trace of prohibition in it and there is nothing on which to rely, it is certainly fitting to abolish the custom by force, and one should not heed the voice of ignorant whisperers who wish to uphold their ancestors' custom without distinguishing between good and bad, opening their mouths without restraint, saying, “Look, new sages have arisen bringing forth a new Torah, things we have never heard with our ears and our fathers never told us. Did we not see [earlier] sages? If it were true, why did such-and-such a sage or such-and-such a sage not say it?” Regarding this our sages, of blessed memory, already said (Chullin 7a) that each person's ancestors left him room to distinguish himself, and therefore a Torah scholar who says something new should not be scorned.
Pele Yoetz 219:2: And would that confused spirits gain wisdom and understanding, for what concern is it to them to be pained over the uprooting of a custom — the sage who uproots the custom should worry about himself, for the sage certainly knows the power of custom better than he does; and if, God forbid, it is a sin, the blame hangs on the neck of the sage, who bears the sin of the many, and the whole congregation is cleared of guilt. And just as they trust the sage on all matters of prohibition and permission, so too it is fitting that they trust him in this, for he knows what he is doing. And it is not always true that “great is the power of custom,” for sometimes a custom is like Gehinnom itself. However, if there is no trace of prohibition in it, or if there is something to rely on, it is fitting to have regard for the custom.
Pele Yoetz 219:3: And it is already written in Sefer Chasidim (section 114) that one who abolishes a piyyut [liturgical poem] that people are accustomed to reciting transgresses “you shall not move the boundary marker” set by the early ones. And if he is God-fearing and wishes to satisfy all opinions, or to observe some custom of piety according to the Ari, of blessed memory, let him conduct himself with a pure heart within his own house, and not display it publicly, unless he is renowned for piety and everyone responds “holy” after him; and he should not protest against others who do not do so, but he should not follow the majority for evil and do as they do, for there is a chronic evil among many unlearned people who transgress matters of Torah and neglect several commandments, such as washing the hands, the third Shabbat meal, communal fasts and the like, and when protested against, they say, “This is how we are accustomed,” and let such a custom disappear — and likewise several bad customs, with neglect of Torah study outweighing them all, which have become as though permitted. Here it is not applicable to follow custom. And if he cannot protest against others, at least, guarding his own soul, he should distance himself from them and not do as they do.
Pele Yoetz 219:4: And even in mundane matters it is not fitting to follow custom, such as in the order of excessive expenditures that people have become accustomed to, where even one whose means do not allow it presses himself and is troubled and made miserable for the sake of honor or because of pressure from his household — for the minds of women are easily swayed — and this is not the straight path; rather, he should be precise in his order of expenditure according to what is essential and according to his means, and should not be concerned about custom, but simply do what is his to do. Even if people speak against him as one who has strayed and are strict with him and voice complaints against him, all this is vanity and vexation of spirit, provided he does not cause strife thereby, especially with members of his own household, but rather guides and leads them with sweet speech and a soft tongue according to his own way, for great is peace.
Pele Yoetz 220:1: Middot (Character Traits) — Good and upright traits, how good and beautiful they are! One who conducts himself with them is beloved above and cherished below, and finds favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man. On the other hand, the punishment for bad traits is severe, and one who conducts himself with them is hated and detestable, evil toward Heaven and evil toward humanity, as explained in the words of our holy sages, of blessed memory, in the Talmud, the Midrashim, the holy Zohar, and the ethical books, which are full of splendor — whoever meditates on them tastes the taste of the fear of sin. For it is true that there are differing dispositions: there is one whom the Lord has graced with a good nature and good traits and proper opinions from the womb and from conception, and there is the complete opposite, God have mercy and grant remedy. And one whom the Lord has graced with understanding, for whom it is easy to conduct himself with good and upright traits and who recognizes the disgrace of bad traits, should give thanks for his portion and say, “I am unworthy of all the kindnesses,” for this kindness is better than life and than all the life of the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 220:2: But what shall the son do whose traits are bad and whose opinions are ugly, who strays from the path of reason and calls evil good and good evil, and whose way is right in his own eyes? This is a chronic evil with no remedy, for King Solomon, peace be upon him, already said (Proverbs 26:12), “You see a man wise in his own eyes; there is more hope for a fool than for him.” Let him do this then, that perhaps he may be saved: pour out his soul before the Lord, uttering speech day by day, evening, morning and noon, within the Amidah prayer (and with God's help I shall lift my hand for this too and include it in my prayer book, with Heaven's help), that He guide him with good counsel to be complete in traits and opinions and in every kind of perfection, and to do what is good and upright in the eyes of God and man. And he should also persist in studying the books that instruct a person, and dust himself in the dust of the feet of the sages and learn from their deeds, and not depart from their words, even if it seems to him that they call left right; let him not rely on his own understanding (Proverbs 3:5), and nullify his own opinion and will before the will of others, and strengthen himself with a mighty hand and outstretched arm, with great vigor, to act against his own nature or opinion for extended periods, until habit becomes his nature, and the Lord opens his eyes and he sees with his own eyes, and his heart understands which is the straight path, and he turns and is healed, for the reward is according to the pain. And it is a tradition that one who comes to purify himself is helped [from Heaven] (Shabbat 104a). But this does not exempt him from the Day of Judgment by saying, “Such was my nature and such was my understanding, and I could not restrain myself and go against my opinion and my nature.” This is not a way to remove him from transgression, for whatever a man desires to do, he can do, and everything is possible through toil and labor. And they already said (Megillah 6b), “If someone tells you, ‘I have labored and not found [success],’ do not believe him,” for man is born to labor. Happy is he whose labor is in Torah and who gives delight to his Creator — this is a great principle in the Torah, and this is the whole of man.
Pele Yoetz 221:1: Machloket (Strife) — It is known how hated strife is, as explained in the words of our holy sages, of blessed memory, and given its severity, how greatly a person must strengthen himself with great vigor to distance himself and flee from it as one flees from death. And behold, one to whom it has not come to engage in strife should not boast, for one may truly boast only when he has great cause to engage in strife — such as when others sin against him in body, money, or honor — and nevertheless he is among those who are insulted but do not insult, who hear their disgrace and do not respond (Shabbat 88b; Gittin 36b), of whom Scripture says (Judges 5:31), “And may those who love Him be like the sun rising in its might.” And it is known what they explained on the verse (Job 26:7), “He hangs the earth on nothing [belimah]” — the world endures only because of one who restrains [bolem] his mouth at a time of quarrel (Chullin 89a). And through our sins, the enemy — the inclination toward strife over trivial matters — has grown strong, for truly it is all vanity and vexation of spirit, for what does it give or add, the honor with which one might honor him, or the disgrace with which a man, who is like a breath, might disgrace him?
Pele Yoetz 221:2: Would that when there is a quarrel between men, one of them, if he were God-fearing and a pursuer of peace, would also bring the other to the ways of peace, for strife cannot endure if it is one-sided; but the difficulty is that “when men strive together,” both are equally at fault, and each one raises himself up saying, “I am greater, why should I lower myself and remain beneath him?” And thereby strife grows and multiplies, for they said (Sanhedrin 7a), “This quarrel is like a river breach — once it flows, it flows [and grows].” And would that confused spirits gain wisdom to understand that one who lowers himself to pursue peace is the one who rises higher and higher.
Pele Yoetz 221:3: And if the evil of strife is great “when men strive together,” how much more so is the doubled and redoubled evil when there is a quarrel between a man and his wife. And it is known how much the Sages labored and how many ordinances they made for the sake of peace, especially for peace in the home. And the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, written in holiness, was permitted to be erased in order to bring peace between a man and his wife, and from this we learn how much a person must endure for the sake of peace in the home. And always, when there are words of strife, wisdom must come from the greater one to rebuke Satan, and he should not hold to the quarrel, but should be a lover of peace and pursuer of peace, all the more so between a man and his wife, since the minds of women are easily swayed, and it is incumbent upon the man, who has understanding, to forgo his own grievance and lower himself for the honor of his Maker and pursue peace with all his strength, for great is the evil of strife within the home, which brings evil upon himself and upon his offspring after him. And woe to one who blemishes his offspring, causing his children to be children of strife, children of a hateful heart.
Pele Yoetz 221:4: Therefore let a man be firm in strengthening himself to seek peace in the home, and a man becomes wealthy as the honor of his house increases. And certainly, all the more so, one should not engage in strife against the community, even if it seems to him that they are wronging him and treating him against the law — the law is with the community, for behold, God is mighty and does not despise (Job 8:20); and if for all transgressions one must build fence upon fence and safeguard upon safeguard, how much more so regarding strife, given its severity. And just as it is said (Psalms 34:15), “Seek peace and pursue it,” likewise distance yourself from strife and flee from it as one flees from fire, for it is a fire that consumes unto destruction.
Pele Yoetz 221:5: And behold, most strife is found among women, for ten men can sit together in love and brotherhood, while no two women can dwell together without strife. And they already said in Avot DeRabbi Natan: when you see white ravens, [then] you will see two sisters dwelling together in peace and friendship — and moreover, they even stir up quarrels among men. Therefore, dispersion [living apart] benefits them and benefits their husbands. And brothers should not dwell together in one house, nor a daughter-in-law with her mother-in-law. And as soon as one sees words of strife approaching, one should immediately separate the bundle before the flame rises, for afterward “a continual fire shall burn, it shall not go out,” since strife leads to insults and curses, and afterward “you have transgressed a lasting guard.” Therefore let one hasten to find escape one hour beforehand, and not worry about increased expense, and not retreat before anything, for strife destroys money, body, and soul, while great is peace, for there the Lord commanded the blessing, life forevermore.
Pele Yoetz 222:1: Muvchar (The Choicest) — How great is the merit of performing a commandment with the choicest, which demonstrates love. And they said in the Talmud, Tractate Berachot (30a), “‘From being good’ [mihyot tov] should not be read [as] ‘evil’ [ra].” Rashi explained: since I am able to do good and perform a commandment with the choicest, I should not call it “evil” not to perform the commandment with the choicest. Learn from this that whoever does not perform a commandment with the choicest is called by an evil name.
Pele Yoetz 222:2: And a person should see how meticulous he is about his own eating and drinking, that it be fatty, well-spiced meat, and fine flour, and good wine in beautiful vessels, and how much effort and expense he puts into his clothing to be well-dressed, never satisfied with what comes readily to hand, always seeking the choicest kind — how much more so should he be meticulous in doing his Maker's will, to give delight to his Creator. And if he is not so satisfied [with less than the best for himself but settles for less in serving God], it is as though he has no regard for his Maker's honor, God forbid, while it is within his power to give more delight to his Creator, as I wrote above under the entry Mitzvot. Therefore, whatever is in his power to do in the best manner, let him do.
Pele Yoetz 223:1: Mishpat V'Din (Judgment and Law) — The virtue of justice is known, as it is written (Isaiah 1:27), “Zion shall be redeemed with justice.” And it is written (Deuteronomy 16:18), “Judges and officers you shall appoint for yourself in all your gates.” One must appoint in every single city a sage who will render rulings on matters of prohibition and permission, and judge between a man and his brother, and inform them of God's statutes and His teachings, and the way in which they should walk and the deeds they should do.
Pele Yoetz 223:2: Now, in order that there be settlement and order in every city, there are warnings that the people of the city must heed and warnings for a judge, and these are matters without fixed measure, for it all depends on the place, the time, the disposition of the judge and his traits, and the opinions and traits of the people, who must conduct themselves with one another and bear with one another so that their partnership turns out well, in love and brotherhood, peace and friendship, like brothers dwelling together. Nevertheless, I shall write some warnings fitting to conduct oneself by — let the wise man hear and add learning. Let us begin with the warning to the community: it is fitting for every community of Israel, even if they are a poor community, to press themselves in this matter to have a head and a leader, so that the congregation of the Lord not be like sheep without a shepherd (Numbers 27:17), for when there is no king in Israel, everyone does what is right and crooked in his own eyes. Whether in matters of prohibition and permission, if there is no one among them who knows, they permit the forbidden and call evil good and good evil — and even if they do so unwittingly, God will bring them into judgment for not having sought someone to teach them while it was in their power, for an unwitting error in learning is elevated to willfulness. Or in monetary matters, there must be a man over the community to rescue the exploited from the hand of his exploiter through the power of the Torah, for were it not for its fear, men would swallow each other alive through our criminal enemies, the gentile courts, which lean toward gain and bribery, besides the severity involved in litigating in gentile courts, as explained by the halachic authorities — it makes a person's hair stand on end.
Pele Yoetz 223:3: And even if they are judged according to Jewish law by men who are not learned in the laws of the Torah, according to human reasoning, they still do not escape judging according to their own eyes' perception, and there is a bias of favor toward friends or toward whoever benefits them, and they do not see it as guilt against themselves; and even if they do what is good and right according to their own understanding, they still do not escape suspicion, but whoever loses his case in judgment will slander and disparage them. In any case, in a place where there are no learned men, it is fitting to choose the lesser evil and appoint God-fearing, understanding merchants to judge between a man and his fellow, so that the children of Israel need not go to gentile courts, God forbid. But happy is the land whose king is a Torah scholar, who renders rulings and saves the city by his wisdom, and his merit protects them, saving them from all evil and bringing blessing upon all the work of their hands; therefore let each man help his fellow, and the weak should say, “I am a hero,” to hold fast to this commandment of establishing a Torah scholar's court in the city. And one commandment leads to another, for included in this is that they should support those who study Torah, and thereby they take a share in his Torah and his deeds, and how good is their portion and how pleasant their lot. But they must press themselves to sufficiently provide for the scholar's needs generously and not sparingly, in such a way that his mind is clear and settled and he is not impoverished. And how good is the portion of those who serve Torah scholars, for their service is greater than their study (Berachot 7b), and at the very hour the Torah scholar is free to teach on their behalf, they take their share. And how, then, is it known whether one whose soul longs for Torah and grieves that his portion is not among those who sit in the study hall is sincere? If his words are true, let him do what is in his power to support those who study Torah, some with their bodies and some with their money, for greater is one who causes [others to do a mitzvah] than one who does it himself (Bava Batra 9a; Massechet Kallah 2). And it is written (Ecclesiastes 7:12), “In the shadow of wisdom, in the shadow of money.” And it is known what they explained on the verse (Deuteronomy 16:20), “Justice, justice shall you pursue” — follow a good court (Sanhedrin 32b).
Pele Yoetz 223:4: Thus the people of the city must take care, before appointing a leader over the community, to examine him very thoroughly, that his reputation be good, that he be a sage expert in the laws of the Torah, that his fear of sin precede his wisdom, and that he be complete in traits and opinions, knowing how to lead the community according to their dispositions and to bear with them as a nurse carries a suckling child (Numbers 11:12). And if there is a Torah scholar among the sons of the city, he takes precedence, for he is more expert in the local regulations and the people's traits and nature, and they are familiar with him and know him. And if they need to bring one from another region, they should make a thorough investigation before accepting him, so that they not come to regret it and increase strife, God forbid. And it is known what our sages, of blessed memory, said on the verse (Deuteronomy 1:18), “And I commanded you at that time” — a warning to the community that they hold the judge in awe (Sanhedrin 8a). And it is written (Deuteronomy 6:13), “You shall revere the Lord your God” — to include Torah scholars (Pesachim 22b). Thus the community must be extra careful not to rebel against the words of the teacher and not to deviate right or left from what he tells them, even if he says of right that it is left or the reverse.
Pele Yoetz 223:5: And the essence of this commandment is incumbent upon the notables of the city, the leaders of the congregation, who have the power to establish and raise the banner of the Torah — they must stand at the right hand of the judge with all their strength and all their might to uphold his words, so that not one of his words falls to the ground; and even if occasionally something improper or uncorrected comes from the judge's hand, since he is human and every man is a liar, the notables of the city must uphold his words and break the teeth of the wicked who speak crookedly and wish to cast off [his authority] and give a stubborn shoulder, refusing to heed his words — they should subdue them and strike them and beat them until they listen and do all that comes from his mouth. Thereby the awe of the judge will be upon them, the banner of the Torah will be raised, and the order and settlement of the city will be good. And those who support the teacher in raising the banner of the Torah, in this the mighty man may boast of his might, as when he performs valor like a man of war, standing guard over the Torah and its service, to serve it, guard it, support it, and sustain it, and they will take their share of good reward, like the share of the one who sits in the seat of ruling.
Pele Yoetz 223:6: And just as they said (Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 65) regarding a wife, “The cause that fell to your lot, good or bad, drag it along [i.e., bear with it],” so too with this matter: if it happens that they have taken as their head a harsh man, prone to anger and harsh traits, the people of the city must accommodate him according to his traits and bear with him, and not provoke him, and not increase strife, God forbid. And let there be awe of the judge upon them, and let them be careful not to be burned by his coal; and needless to say, they should not cast off the yoke from their neck and remove him from his position, for then the congregation of the Lord would be like sheep without a shepherd (Numbers 11:12), unable to find someone to fill his place, since people would fear the same thing happening again.
Pele Yoetz 223:7: And I have already said that great is the evil of a city that has no teacher — they walk in darkness with no light for them. Therefore, even if they lack the means to have a rabbi, a moreh tzedek [halachic authority], they should not fail to obtain a cantor or teacher who knows how to read, somewhat expert in the laws of prohibition and permission, to teach ethical books, so that they not be like the ugly ones who walk in darkness, God forbid; and they should be careful of his honor, since he is like a rose among thorns, and in a place of the blind, one with a single eye must be esteemed — and certainly one must be careful of the honor of the rabbi, the moreh tzedek, both because he is a Torah scholar and because he is a judge.
Pele Yoetz 223:8: And it is known what our sages, of blessed memory, said (Sanhedrin 99b), that one who shames his fellow in the presence of a Torah scholar is called a heretic — not to mention how the affliction has spread, where when standing before the court people curse and revile one another in the presence of the sage, and would that they would not disgrace the sage himself when he rules against them in judgment, or when he rebukes them to their face for having done wrong, for the way of a fool is right in his own eyes, and he considers himself wiser than the sage, thinking the sage has treated him improperly and not according to the strict line of the law. Woe to a generation upon whom such things have fallen in its days. And it is already known, the saying of our sages, of blessed memory (Yalkut Shimoni there), on the verse “And it came to pass in the days when the judges judged” (Ruth 1:1) — woe, in the days when they judge their judges! “And there was a famine in the land,” Heaven have mercy. And even if the judges are ordinary merchants, one must be careful of their honor, for even the head of a caravan is appointed from Heaven (Bava Batra 91b), and when three sit in judgment, the Divine Presence is among them (Berachot 6a), as it is said (Psalms 82:1), “In the midst of the judges He judges” — and according to the law, their status is like that of Torah scholars, and one who disgraces them is like one who disgraces Torah scholars, as explained by the halachic authorities, and of them it is said (I Samuel 2:30), “And those who despise Me shall be lightly esteemed.” And of one who honors them it is said (ibid.), “For those who honor Me I will honor.”
Pele Yoetz 223:9: And it is incumbent upon all members of the community not to give aid to transgressors, and even toward his own father and mother he should say, “I have not seen him,” and not recognize his brother, and not know his children, even if it seems to him that they have wronged them and rendered a crooked judgment — he should not heed him to say such things to them, God forbid, but rather rebuke and admonish them with the spirit of his lips and say to them, “Whatever the rabbi, the moreh tzedek, or whoever is the judge of our time has done, we accept and are satisfied, for we have only the judge of our own days, to whom you shall listen, for whatever God places in their understanding they will do, and judgment belongs to God.” And if the community does not support the judges and teachers, it is the sin of the community, causing the city to be destroyed, God forbid; but if they stand at the right hand of their righteousness to uphold their words with full strength, unwavering, that city will prosper from the blessing of the Lord — “give her the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates” (Proverbs 31:31).
Pele Yoetz 223:10: And the obligation is even greater upon the Torah scholars of the city to raise the horn of the moreh tzedek, and not to make themselves like advocates who teach litigants arguments for the sake of monetary gain, God forbid, for this causes many evils, increasing strife in Israel and casting suspicion among Torah scholars, disgrace of the Torah and its students, giving a bad odor to them and to the moreh tzedek — and the desecration of the Name is worse than all of these. And the flame of the fire of strife breaks forth and rises to the very heart of the heavens, and people will say of them, “those who pursue lewdness draw near” (Psalms 119:150), like harlots who adorn one another (Shabbat 34a), and they have distanced themselves from Your Torah. And of them it is said (Song of Songs 2:15), “Catch us the foxes,” etc. Therefore happy are the innocent of way, who walk in the Torah of the Lord (Psalms 119:1), who do not involve themselves in any business, judgment, or matter of the city's affairs.
Pele Yoetz 223:11: And even if his brother or relative has a court case, and it seems to him that the law is on his side and the moreh tzedek is erring in judgment and convicting the innocent party, he should make himself like a mute, not opening his mouth, and should not even go to say to the moreh tzedek, “Teach me from where you derived your ruling, for it is Torah and I need to learn it,” for in this orphaned generation, one who does this will not escape hatred and rivalry. And one who withholds himself from [interfering in] the judgment releases enmity and blame from himself, while one who is arrogant in rendering rulings is a fool, wicked, and haughty of spirit. And needless to say, he should not go about as a talebearer and reveal his secret [opinion] to the litigant, saying to him, “In my opinion, the law is with you,” for this causes great evil; rather he should say to him, “I do not concern myself with this even if you give me all the silver and gold in the world; rather, go to the moreh tzedek, and whatever he tells you to do, do, not deviating right or left.” This is the way of Torah scholars who increase peace in the world, and thereby they find favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man, and the honor of Heaven is increased and the honor of the Torah and its students is magnified. These are some of the upright paths fitting for the people of the city who desire the settlement and betterment of the city to conduct themselves by. And now let us speak a little of which is the straight path that one who sits on the seats of judgment should choose for himself.
Pele Yoetz 223:12: Let us first say that given the severity and the great burden and the essential danger involved for one who sits in the seat of judgment, from several aspects: on the one hand, he could err in judgment, in a ruling, and in weighing the matter, and could stumble into permitting the forbidden and forbidding the permitted, purifying the impure and defiling the pure, convicting the innocent and acquitting the guilty, and he casts down many victims, in such a way that “the offering between his thighs is destroyed” and Gehinnom is open beneath him; and on the other hand, he is prone to flatter and not protest against those he has the power to protest against, which is bearing the sin of the many; and on the other hand, if he wishes to act according to what is right, he will not escape strife, enmity, and other such evils, to the point that they said (Pesachim 87b), “Woe to the rabbinate, which buries its holders,” Heaven have mercy.
Pele Yoetz 223:13: Thus it is fitting for a Torah scholar to be troubled and let it be well for him, and to flee very far from the rabbinate, and it is better to be a digger of graves than to be a rabbi, a moreh tzedek. However, if it is decreed upon him from Heaven — since even the head of a caravan is appointed from Heaven (Bava Batra 91b), and the Holy One, blessed be He, already showed Moses each generation and its judges (Bamidbar Rabbah 23:5) — and how, then, is it known if it is decreed upon him from Heaven? When he finds himself in a place where there are no [suitable] men, who are like sheep without a shepherd, and they rise up against him and press him persistently to be their head and leader, teaching them the way in which they should walk, in such a way that he flees from honor and honor pursues him — this is a sign and a wonder that the matter came from the Lord. And in such a case it is a commandment to bring merit to the many, if he is capable of it, for they already said (Avodah Zarah 19b), “‘And mighty are all her slain’ — this refers to a Torah scholar who has reached the level of rendering rulings but does not render them.” But let him do this, then: perhaps this will bring him some salvation — this comes first, that he precede with prayer at a time of trouble and pour out his soul before the Lord that He guide him with good counsel from before Him and save him from every error and every mishap, and that nothing uncorrected come from his hand, and likewise for every matter needed according to its place and time, let him open his mouth wide and ask of our God, from the mercy of the One who hears the voice of the prayer of His people Israel with compassion. (And I have already composed a prayer for this and included it in my prayer book, with Heaven's help.)
Pele Yoetz 223:14: And second, let him do this: that he review the laws again and again, both outside the time of an actual case and at the time of an actual case, until he becomes expert in them in all their details and fine points, and examine the depth of the law until it becomes as clear to him as his own sister, and not compare one matter to another lightly. And if there are Torah scholars in the city, he should discuss it with them so that a beam-worthy [strong] result be reached, and not judge alone by his own opinion. And if the geniuses of the world, the sages of the Talmud, did this (Sanhedrin 7b), we, orphans of orphans of shallow knowledge, what shall we say after them? For if in a matter where there are different sides and room for doubt, one relies on his own knowledge, though he has someone to ask and does not ask, this is included in being arrogant in rendering rulings, God forbid.
Pele Yoetz 223:15: And he should also do this: stipulate with the people of the community that they will be satisfied with whatever he rules and judges, even if he errs in a matter of Mishnah [an explicit ruling], that they forgive him. And this is helpful regarding monetary loss, for any condition regarding money is valid, and at least it takes away half [the liability]. And it is fitting for the people of the city to agree to this and have regard for their rabbi's soul, that he not go to Gehinnom on their account, for even though they agree, it is still incumbent upon the judge to examine and search as far as he is able — nevertheless it is done and it helps, so that if in spite of all this he errs because on some occasion he did not examine thoroughly and did not do what he should have done, he will not be punished on their account.
Pele Yoetz 223:16: And there is another great fence regarding monetary law, which is a great field of Torah: that he not insist on strict Torah law, but strive with all his strength to arrange a compromise close to the strict law, in a manner good and right in the eyes of God and man, so that each man returns to his place in peace. And even this he should not do alone, but rather join with him, from time to time, the notables of the city — merchants, men of truth, of great understanding, expert in the ways of business and in the character of the townspeople — and through this a proper judgment will emerge, a true judgment of truth, and they will be a help to him so that his words are heeded, and no one will be found to rebel or suspect the one who hears it. And truly they said (Ecclesiastes 4:9), “Two are better than one.”
Pele Yoetz 223:17: And how good and pleasant it would be if it were established in every city that every judgment and law be judged by the rabbi, the moreh tzedek, together with the notables and leaders of the city, according to law and according to what is right, and enact by the agreement of the townspeople that no one shall rebel and none shall deviate from what they say, even if they call right left. And the teacher must be complete in his traits, and conduct himself according to the place and the time, and according to the person and the matter and the need of the hour — sometimes he must speak harshly and cast bile, showing an angry face on the outside, but he must guard himself with extra care that his heart within remain calm and empty [of real anger], and not come to actual anger, so as not to come to error (their advice was rejected [an idiom for a failed attempt]), and sometimes a soft tongue breaks a bone. And he must be very patient, bearing the burden of the community on his neck without wilting, leading the congregation like sheep, and even if they are troublesome, stubborn, and insulting to him, he should lead and guide them with pleasant speech and a sweet palate.
Pele Yoetz 223:18: And especially when the litigants stand before him, he must be careful and take heed not to become angry with either of them, even if one steps out of line and behaves improperly and speaks harshly, words as harsh as sinews — this is not a time for anger, whether because there is concern that this will silence his arguments, or because if he loses the case, the judge may be suspected of having judged him unfavorably out of enmity, God forbid. Moreover, one should not blame too much the one who gives a stubborn shoulder and speaks harshly when he loses the case, for according to his own understanding, it seemed to him that the law was on his side, and when he loses, his anger and jealousy flare, for the blood is the life, and he cannot restrain himself from speaking harshly — not from his heart, for his heart is not with him. Know that the rabbi will regret this afterward; therefore is it not better that he wait until that moment passes, and afterward rebuke him to his face for having acted improperly, when he will be more easily appeased? And sometimes he should make himself as though deaf, not hearing, and as though he did not know, for it is known that even among the nations, regarding Israel (Beitzah 25b), “And the people spoke against God and against Moses” (Numbers 21:5). And the Holy One, blessed be He, already commanded Moses to bear the burden of the people as a nurse carries a suckling child (Numbers 11:12), and said to him, “My children are troublesome and stubborn; it is on this condition that you accept them upon yourselves” (Yalkut, Va'era, remez 178), and thereby the reward of the leaders is increased.
Pele Yoetz 223:19: And further, the teacher's heart must be like a lion's heart: he should not flatter, should not favor the poor, and should not honor the great, but let judgment pierce through the mountain (Sanhedrin 7b) — he should not retreat before anything, and should not have regard for the diminishment of his own honor or benefit, for those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing. And he should investigate and inquire and study thoroughly, searching as far as he is able, to know what is happening in the city, deeds that should not be done, and he should close the breaches of the city, and enact ordinances and upright practices according to the need of the hour, with a spirit of knowledge and fear of the Lord. And if he finds a man or men who are worthless, transgressing sinners, stepping out of line, he should rebuke them with the rod of his tongue, and if they do not listen, he should further strike them a heavy blow and pursue them to the point of destruction, for when there is no judgment below, there is judgment above, God forbid; and he should not fear any man (Deuteronomy 1:17), but do his deeds for the sake of Heaven, for the honor of his Rock, and He will be his help and his mighty one, and let everything proceed in proper order by the counsel of the officers and deputies, for salvation lies in an abundance of counselors (Proverbs 11:14), and “one who listens to counsel is wise” (ibid. 12:15). And we already find (Sanhedrin 38b) that the Holy One, blessed be He, took counsel with the ministering angels in order to teach the people that the great should take counsel from the small, and sometimes in the wrapping of a poor man one finds a pearl (Zohar, part 3, p. 157b). And the teacher must also expound to the people God's statutes and His teachings and the way of life, ethical rebuke, for perhaps his words will bear fruit, at least, if not for a hundred, or for ten, then at least for one.
Pele Yoetz 223:20: And further, the teacher's eyes must be open toward the poor of the city and toward travelers, and especially toward the Torah scholars of the city, he should have regard for them as for his own body, and inquire to know of their distress and how they make their living, and strive with all his strength to bring them benefit, and gently press the people of the city regarding charity, to give to each man according to what he is and according to his need, and according to the blessing the Lord has given them, that by doing what they should do, they may bring blessing to their houses. The teacher must also mingle with the people of the city, rejoicing in their joy and suffering in all their trouble, and seek mercy on behalf of the community and the individual, that they be saved from their trouble and from every trouble that might come upon them, and that they be satisfied and full of the Lord's blessing, for it is already known (Makkot 11a) that the High Priest was punished in the matter of exile to the cities of refuge for not having sought mercy on behalf of his generation — and certainly one who dwells in the city and benefits from its people must not be ungrateful, and should do whatever is in his power to do, for in the peace of the city he will have peace, and the essential point is for the honor of the Divine Presence, for at a time when Israel is in distress, the Divine Presence is distressed, God forbid.
Pele Yoetz 223:21: And in order that the rabbinate not “bury its holder,” Heaven have mercy, one must be careful not to conduct oneself in the manner of authority, and not to go about with matters too great and wondrous for oneself, and when honored, he should take to heart his own smallness according to the scale and balance of justice that belongs to the Lord, as stated above under the entry Ga'avah [Pride], and to be further explained under the entry Anavah [Humility], and should not enjoy the honor. And it is known the saying of our sages, of blessed memory (Sanhedrin 14a), “Accept and fulfill.” These are some points of the straight path that one who sits in judgment should walk in. Let the wise man hear and add learning.
Pele Yoetz 223:22: And I further speak regarding the conduct of litigants, for it is true that our Sages said, “Whoever loses his cloak in court should sing and go away [i.e., accept the loss gracefully]” (Sanhedrin 7a), but our eyes see the complete opposite — that as soon as he is summoned to a Torah court, his anger and wrath flare, and he becomes his opponent's enemy and foe, and this is nothing but a lack of understanding, for what does it matter if people come to seek God? However, according to the custom of people, it is fitting for one who wishes to be a seeker of peace and pursuer of peace to withhold his hand, as much as he can, from summoning his fellow to a Torah court, and to strive to settle the matter through beloved friends; and if in any case he cannot avoid summoning him to judgment, he should first go to him and speak words of peace, saying, “My brother and my friend, let it not seem evil to you, for we are brothers, and my heart is whole with you in love and brotherhood, only that we differ in opinion, and both of us want the truth and what is right, only a third party must come and decide between us. Let us arise and go seek God in peace and uprightness, and we shall be careful to do all that they instruct us.” And when they come before the judge, let them present their arguments calmly, in a low voice, and let neither interrupt the other's words, and whoever loses the case should accept the judgment upon himself with love and rejoice that the stolen item has left his hand, and afterward let them be beloved friends as before.
